title: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us
summary: Is keeping a family business together always worth the cost?

blocks.text: What happens when the people you inherited a business with are also the people you can no longer work with? You can quit a job, sell your shares, or find a new business partner. But what if that partner is your brother, sister, cousin, or parent, and the company is something your grandparents spent their lives building?

I have covered Philippine business families for most of my journalism career, interviewing relatives locked in battles over ownership, leadership, inheritance, and family land. Some disputes were already playing out in court, while others were waged quietly behind closed boardroom doors even as the companies kept running. As the feud between cousins Federico “Piki” Lopez and Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III unfolded this year, I found myself returning to those stories, my interview notes, and reading Harvard Business Review research on why family businesses fight and how some survive. In June, I joined family-business adviser Enrique Soriano in an online forum with business owners across Asia to discuss why even wildly successful dynasties break apart.

The Lopez cousins are hardly the first wealthy family to face this problem. India’s Ambani brothers split up the Reliance empire their father built, while the Ortigases fought over control of their real estate business. In Singapore, a father accused his son of trying to take over the board of one of the country’s biggest property developers. Some families eventually called a truce. Others decided they could no longer be business partners, and still fought for years, burning through cash on lawyers and leaving the next generation to clean up the mess.
All of this brought me back to one big question: Is keeping a family business together always worth the cost?

For decades, the Lopez name has been tied to some of the Philippines’ most famous companies: ABS-CBN, Meralco, Benpres (now Lopez Holdings), First Philippine Holdings, First Gen, and Rockwell Land. The businesses changed over time, yet the family stayed connected to an empire their elders built, lost, won back, and rebuilt.

Under Oscar Lopez‘s leadership, the family published Phoenix, a book about how they bounced back from hard times. Piki wanted a different symbol for the next chapter: not the phoenix, which rises again after being destroyed, but the butterfly, which transforms into something completely new. He has also talked a lot about compounding, the idea that smart decisions made consistently over decades pay off far more than quick wins. In his September speeches to stockholders, he stressed that “direction matters more than speed,” pointing to the group’s decision ten years earlier to stop building coal-fired power plants even when coal was still making good money.

That mindset explains Piki’s game plan for First Gen’s energy investments. He believes the company must prepare for a power market that relies more and more on renewable energy. His cousins have questioned whether the bets he’s making are worth the massive price tag, risks, and years of waiting. They have also challenged his authority to make those calls on his own. Gabby and his allied cousins wanted something very different: immediate cash flow and shared family stewardship over a distressed media mission—ABS-CBN—that could not afford to wait until 2031 for long-gestation hydro projects to pay off.

blocks.caption: EXCLUSIVE: Inside Piki Lopez’s town hall as cousins rally for ABS-CBN

blocks.text: The fight turned public and personal. In April, majority owners of Lopez Inc.—representing three of the four branches of the family—accused Piki of acting “like a king without accountability,” questioning First Gen’s deals with Enrique Razon Jr.’s Prime Infrastructure, including selling control of its natural-gas business and investing in water-pumping hydropower projects. The majority group later called the hydropower bet “a horrible deal.” First Gen pushed back on those claims, defending the business logic, pricing, and board approvals behind its deals.

The cousins reached a ceasefire in May, but it didn’t hold, and by August, Gabby’s branch sold its 25.68% share in Lopez Inc., the private holding company sitting at the very top of the family empire, to businessman Ramon Ang for about P11.56 billion. Meanwhile, ABS-CBN lined up fresh funding. Piki then locked down control of the boards of Lopez Holdings and First Philippine Holdings (FPH), the two companies that hold the group’s stakes in First Gen and geothermal giant Energy Development Corporation (EDC). In November, FPH approved the proposed P15.92-billion sale of its 90.74% controlling stake in Rockwell Land to Gabby’s branch’s investment firm, Crème Investment Corporation, a deal that is still waiting to close. (READ: What it took to save ABS-CBN)
Taken together, these deals suggest the cousins are moving toward a future where they no longer have to agree on how to run the same businesses.
But is splitting up actually better than staying together?

One family owner wants bigger cash payouts today, while the relative running the company wants to plow back those profits into growing the business. Another thinks they should sell the company while buyers are offering a good price, while someone else wants to save it for the grandkids. One wants to ride out an industry slump, convinced a struggling business will bounce back, while another wants to stop pouring money into what looks like a sinking ship, especially when that cash could fund a different business that takes years of heavy spending before turning a profit.

Yet each walks away believing the others are greedy, reckless, or unreasonable. The real trouble starts when the people around the boardroom table aren’t just ordinary investors, but siblings who grew up competing for their parents’ and uncles’ attention, cousins who feel their branch of the family sacrificed more, or heirs who remember the founder’s wishes differently.

Josh Baron and Rob Lachenauer, who advise business families and write for Harvard Business Review, explain how everyday business arguments turn deeply personal. In Why Fights Erupt in Family Businesses, they show how fights over money, power, and status get tangled up with family history. An argument over company spending can bring back old resentment over unequal treatment. A fight over who gets to be CEO can reopen old arguments about favoritism. Selling a company might look like a smart opportunity to one relative and a betrayal of the family legacy to another.

Soriano raised another complication during our webinar: many family businesses stay united for decades simply because one strong founder or family elder can settle all the arguments. Relatives might not like every decision, yet they accept the leader’s authority. Once that leader passes away, the next generation realizes it has inherited not only the businesses, but also old disagreements that were never truly resolved.

The Lopezes had larger-than-life leaders in Eugenio “Geny” Lopez Jr. and his brother Oscar, who died in 1999 and 2023, leaving their successors to figure out how to own and run surviving empires without those strong elders around to settle arguments.
Other Philippine families have ended up in far messier wars.

Take Banco Filipino, once the country’s biggest savings bank, famous for its slogan, “Subok na Matibay, Subok na Matatag (Tested Strong, Proven Stable).” Founded by Tomas Aguirre in 1964, the bank was shut down by the Central Bank in January 1985 before reopening in 1994 after the Supreme Court ruled the Central Bank had abused its power. But its headaches were far from over. It kept clashing with regulators over financial aid, its money troubles, and the fallout from its first shutdown.

blocks.caption: BANCO FILIPINO. This spread in Newsbreak’s March 3, 2003 issue shows the late Don Tomas Aguirre (left) and his children, Ana Marie Aguirre-Koruga (upper right), and Albert “Bobby” Aguirre (bottom right) on a polo field. Rappler

blocks.text: At the same time, the Aguirre family was tearing itself apart from the inside. I covered the legal fight involving Ana Maria Aguirre-Koruga, a minority stockholder who sued the bank’s directors in 2003, including her own brother, Albert Aguirre, who was then vice chairman. She accused them of risky banking practices, conflicts of interest, and shady loans meant to enrich insiders. The directors denied the claims. In 2009, the Supreme Court ruled in Koruga v. Arcenas that her complaints belonged with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), not a regular trial court. That ruling only decided who had authority to hear the case, not whether her accusations were true. The bank shut down for good on March 17, 2011, under BSP orders. The state deposit insurer, Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation, took over a bank with 62 branches, 173,480 accounts, and P17.8 billion in customer deposits. The family and regulators kept arguing over who was to blame. While the sibling feud wasn’t the sole reason Banco Filipino collapsed—its financial and regulatory problems ran much deeper—the family war played out inside a bank holding the life savings of thousands of ordinary Filipinos.

The Ilusorio family feud got even more personal. Potenciano “Nanoy” Ilusorio built a multi-billion-peso empire anchored by prime real estate, the pioneering satellite firm Philcomsat, and the exclusive Baguio Country Club. But by 1999, his six children had split into rival camps over their parents, the family fortune, and who should be in charge. When Nanoy grew old and frail, some of his children took him under their care, prompting their mother, Erlinda Kalaw-Ilusorio, to sue them for allegedly keeping her husband away from her, a battle the Supreme Court dismissed in 2001 as the “sad tale of a prominent family shattered by conflicts on expectancy in fabled fortune.” (READ: What drives people to declare war against their own flesh and blood?)

Even Nanoy’s death in June that year didn’t stop nearly 300 civil and criminal lawsuits filed between the rival camps, and according to an account Soriano published in 2016, some children only found out of Erlinda’s death four days later, leading to separate funerals. At one service, the urn reportedly held Nanoy’s ashes because another branch of the family kept Erlinda’s. Another service reportedly barred three of the sisters at the door with security guards.
A fight that started over money and power had reached the point where children could not even mourn their parents together.

In other prominent Philippine clans, the fracture began not at a parent’s deathbed, but when siblings began questioning how a brother or sister was managing inherited assets—turning boardroom suspicions into criminal complaints and proxy wars.

For the Jacintos, who built their wealth in steel, banking, and real estate, also fought over their inheritance. After their patriarch, Fernando Jacinto died, his children clashed over how family properties were being managed and sold. Musician and businessman Ramon “RJ” Jacinto stepped in after relatives questioned real estate deals handled by their sister Marilene, who was running parts of the family business. One fight centered on a large property in Misamis Oriental sold in 2007 for P226 million, which RJ’s camp argued was far below its appraised value. Another involved a Novaliches property reportedly worth about P300 million. Acting as president of family-owned Oregon Land Inc., RJ accused Marilene of faking a deed to transfer the land. Prosecutors charged her in 2012 with falsifying public documents, an accusation that led to criminal proceedings, though not a conviction. The feud showed how inheritance fights can quickly spiral into claims of betrayal and criminal charges between brothers and sisters. (READ: Shaping the future: Family legacies)

blocks.caption: Family feud: Court ruling saves Olivia Yanson’s share in PH’s biggest transport fleet

blocks.text: In the Yanson family, the trigger was a boardroom ouster over who would run the business. They parents founded Vallacar Transit Inc. and the Ceres bus empire, considered among the largest bus conglomerates in Southeast Asia with about 5,000 buses ferrying 700,000 to 850,000 passengers in routes across Visayas and Mindanao regions. In July 2019, four siblings—Roy, Emily, Ricardo Jr., and Ma. Lourdes Celina Yanson-Lopez—tried to oust their youngest brother, Leo Rey Yanson, from running the bus group. Their mother, Olivia Yanson, sided with Leo Rey and Ginette, splitting the family into Yanson 4 and Yanson 2 camps. They fought over who had the right to elect board directors and run the company, triggering lawsuits and battles over company records. In 2025, the Supreme Court said Olivia was mentally sound when she executed her will that designated the Yanson 2 camp as the righful heirs of their family business empire. The family still hasn’t reached the kind of broad peace deal needed to put the feud behind them. (READ: Yanson family feud gets uglier as court brands 4 siblings ‘fugitives from justice’)

This family drama resonated elsewhere in Asia where South Korea’s Lotte Group—the retail, hospitality, and confectionery giant behind Asia’s largest department stores, luxury hotels, and iconic snacks—became the stage for a succession war between brothers Shin Dong-joo and Shin Dong-bin, sons of founder Shin Kyuk-ho. The business giant had major operations in both Japan and South Korea. Dong-joo, the older brother, was prominent in Japan, while Dong-bin ran much of the Korean side. After Dong-joo lost top posts in Japan in late 2014 and early 2015, the brothers erupted into a public war over who had their father’s blessing and who should lead the empire. Their elderly father was pulled straight into the crossfire. At one point, Shin Kyuk-ho backed his eldest son, prompting Dong-bin’s camp to question whether their father was still mentally fit to make decisions. The brothers battled through shareholder votes, lawsuits, and press statements, turning their father’s mental health and legal guardianship into a court case. Dong-bin eventually won over shareholders and kept control, though Dong-joo kept fighting him. Instead of splitting the empire in two, one brother walked away with control of the main group.

blocks.caption: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

blocks.text: The Shin feud proved a hard truth: being the founder’s son, even being the oldest, doesn’t guarantee inheriting the throne.

In Singapore, the Kwek family— the powers behind iconic skyscrapers, luxury condos, and over 160 hotels worldwide—showed how quickly a disagreement between a father and son could move from the family boardroom into the headlines. In February 2025, City Developments executive chairman Kwek Leng Beng accused his son, chief executive Sherman Kwek, of attempting a boardroom “coup” by bypassing governance rules to appoint independent directors, prompting the elder Kwek to go to court to fire his son. Trading in City Developments shares was suspended as the confrontation became public. For a listed property developer, the dispute raised questions that went beyond the relationship between father and son: Who had the authority to appoint directors? Were corporate procedures being followed? And could the company continue operating effectively while its chairman and chief executive were fighting?

Yet the confrontation ended relatively quickly. On March 12, 2025, City Developments announced that the court proceedings had been settled and would be discontinued. Kwek Leng Beng remained executive chairman and Sherman remained chief executive, while the two newly appointed independent directors whose appointments had sparked the dispute, Jennifer Duong Young and Wong Su-Yen, stepped down. Singapore’s Straits Times later reported that trusted family friends and senior figures had helped mediate the truce. The company continued under the same family leadership, although the settlement did not necessarily mean that every personal disagreement had been resolved.

Here in the Philippines, the Ortigas family—the landed dynasty behind Ortigas Center and Greenhills—also managed to save its core property business after years of infighting. At stake was OCLP Holdings, which controls prime Ortigas land, Greenhills Shopping Center, and Tiendesitas. To gain an edge, rival branches teamed up with competing giants: the Rafael Ortigas group with Ayala Land, and the Francisco Ortigas group with SM Prime Holdings. The battle spilled into court over board elections and whether nominees tied to a rival developer could hold seats.

Those divisions let Ayala and SM deepen their footholds in a fractured enterprise. In November 2014, the developers and Ortigas factions dropped their lawsuits and agreed to work together. The family kept its landholdings intact rather than carving them up, though peace came at a steep price: bringing in powerful giants handed outsiders major influence over an empire that had belonged to the Ortigas family for generations.

There are strong business reasons to keep a family group intact. Companies under common ownership can share cash, talent, bank relationships, and leadership, allowing a stronger sister company to help a struggling one survive a rough patch or undertake massive investments too large for one branch alone. There is also the pull of family history, where a business built by a grandfather means far more to his grandkids than an ordinary stock investment, making a sale feel like erasing part of the family identity even when the financial math makes sense.
Yet keeping a company together merely because the founder wanted it kept together can create another problem: What happens when the next generation no longer agrees on what the business should do?

Adviser Josh Baron has argued in Why Family Businesses Need to Find the Right Level of Conflict that avoiding disagreement is actually unhealthy. Families must debate tough questions rather than letting owners quietly stew over decisions they feel powerless to change. When relatives can still negotiate and compromise, staying together preserves huge value. But when every investment, dividend payout, job appointment, or asset sale becomes another war for control, the cost becomes far too high.
India’s Ambani family decided that the brothers were simply better off running different companies. (READ: Timeline: Key dates in India’s Ambani brothers’ dispute)

After founder Dhirubhai Ambani died in 2002 without leaving a will, his sons Mukesh and Anil fought publicly over who would control Reliance Industries—India’s largest private-sector conglomerate, spanning petrochemicals, refining, telecom, and retail—until their mother, Kokilaben, stepped in to broker a June 2005 peace deal. Mukesh kept Reliance Industries and its core oil and chemical operations, while Anil took charge of telecom, power, and financial services. But it didn’t stop every argument as the brothers later fought over natural-gas supply deals in a battle that reached India’s Supreme Court. Still, they no longer had to agree on every single investment or management call.

India’s Bajaj family—one of the country’s oldest business dynasties, famous for putting India on wheels as a motorcycle, scooter, and financial services powerhouse—also split up its companies among different branches after years of fighting. Under a 2008 settlement, Shishir Bajaj’s branch took control of businesses like Bajaj Hindusthan and Bajaj Consumer Care, while other family branches kept the group’s core auto, finance, and industrial companies.

blocks.caption: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

blocks.text: Splitting up let each branch follow its own game plan. Their paths quickly diverged: the core Bajaj businesses boomed, while Bajaj Hindusthan struggled with heavy debt and a tough sugar market. Dividing the empire ended the fight over who was in charge, but it didn’t guarantee that both sides would win.

In Hong Kong, Walter Kwok was pushed out as leader of Sun Hung Kai Properties—the real estate titan behind the city’s tallest skyscrapers, luxury malls, and housing estates—in 2008 after clashing with his brothers Thomas and Raymond over how to run the empire. The battle pulled in their mother, Kwong Siu-hing, and tangled up the family trusts. Walter lost his executive job, though he didn’t lose his financial slice of the family fortune. He went on to start his own property company, Empire Group Holdings, while new trust rules spelled out each brother’s share of the family wealth.

Taking a different path is the Murdoch family—the real-life inspiration behind HBO’s hit drama Succession, and the media dynasty behind Fox News, The Wall Street Journal, and major outlets across the US, UK, and Australia that have shaped elections and public debate for decades. After a court battle over the family trust controlling voting power in Fox Corporation and News Corp, a September 2025 settlement locked in Lachlan Murdoch’s future control. His three older siblings from 95-year-old Rupert Murdoch‘s first two marriages—Prudence MacLeod, Elisabeth Murdoch, and James Murdoch—walked away with huge payouts and exited the trust. Grace and Chloe, Murdoch’s two youngest daughters from his third wife, Wendi Deng, stayed on as financial beneficiaries under the new setup, but without the voting power given to Lachlan.

Each of these families handled their split differently. The Ambanis and Bajajs divided up operating companies. Walter Kwok stepped out of management while keeping a financial stake. The Murdochs rewrote who holds voting control over their media empire. None of them offers a one-size-fits-all recipe for solving family feuds.

blocks.caption: ADVICE. Enrique Soriano, family business consultant of the Wong & Bernstein  Group, speaks during a forum. Courtesy of the Wong & Bernstein Group

blocks.text: Enrique Soriano, who has advised business families across the Philippines and Asia, does not view such separations as failures, noting during our June webinar that relatives who can no longer work together are often better served by an orderly division of business interests so they can stop being business partners without stopping being family.

Of course, that is much easier said than done. A family deciding to split still has to agree on who gets what, how much each company is worth, who takes on the debts, and what happens to shared properties. One relative might want out, only to find the others can’t afford to buy their shares. Another might want to keep control, but has to bring in an outside investor to help pay for the buyout.
And a peace deal that satisfies the relatives doesn’t automatically work out for the everyday public investors who also have money riding on those companies.

The Lopez cousins appear to be heading toward a more permanent split of their business interests, though whether that turns out well for their companies, outside stockholders, and the family itself will take years to see.
Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled itPart 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN strugglesPart 3 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

Other business dynasties offer no easy answers: The Kweks and Ortigases found ways to keep their shared businesses intact after fierce battles, though both had to make major compromises. The Ambanis and Bajajs carved up their empires. The Kwoks and Murdochs separated day-to-day control from financial ownership. The Shin brothers’ succession war left one brother running Lotte, while the Aguirres, Ilusorios, Jacintos, and Yansons showed how family fights can spiral into years of lawsuits and lasting broken relationships and personal wounds.

There is a world of difference between keeping a company together because the owners actually agree on its future, and keeping it together just because nobody wants to be blamed for breaking up the family empire. There is also a difference between splitting up to chase new ambitions and splitting it up just to stop a fight.

For the Lopezes, going their separate ways may give each branch the freedom to focus on what it values most. Piki can concentrate on long-term energy bets, while Gabby and his allies can focus on lifestyle-related consumer and media businesses. Yet, that freedom brings new pressures, and success will depend on the choices each side makes next.

A family can survive a corporate divorce. Its companies might even grow stronger because of it. Or the split could leave both sides worse off than before. But the real question isn’t just whether relatives should stay together or go their separate ways. It is whether the businesses, and all the people who depend on them, will actually be better off afterward. – Rappler.com
